passage: Gargi stirred her tea and spoke to her old college friend on the balcony. "It's Trisha. First she missed the inter-school quiz, a headache. Then her cousin's engagement. Then the class picnic. Every time, I said, fine, stay home, because if I pushed she'd cry, and the house would be tense all evening. Her father even started calling the school to say she was unwell. I told myself I was being kind. Last month her best friend stopped calling. And I realised I've been helping the fear, not Trisha. So last Sunday I tried something else. I said, 'You don't have to go to the whole birthday lunch. Just come with me for twenty minutes. If it's too much, we'll leave together.' She went pale, but she came. We stayed thirty. I told her I was proud of her for trying. I'm Gargi, and I'm learning that shielding her isn't the same as helping."

qa.q: How long did Gargi and Trisha stay at the birthday lunch?
qa.a: They stayed thirty minutes.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling when she let Trisha stay home each time?
qa.a: Gargi felt worried and wanted to keep the peace, but she now feels uneasy and a little guilty, seeing that saying yes each time was helping the fear.

qa.q: What changed in Gargi's approach, and why is it likely to help?
qa.a: Instead of rescuing Trisha or pushing her, Gargi offered a small, time-limited step with a way out, then praised the effort, which builds Trisha's belief she can cope.

qa.q: What might Trisha be experiencing when she goes pale but comes anyway?
qa.a: Trisha is probably frightened, yet trusting Gargi's promise to leave together lets her try, and staying longer may leave her quietly proud.

grounding: Shows a parent who has been accepting excuses and accommodating a teen's fear, then kindly encouraging a small step instead of rescuing her.

passage:
[Wednesday, 10:52 pm]
Kashish: bhaiya are you awake
Eshaan: ya. what happened
Kashish: will the results tomorrow be okay?
Eshaan: yes. you studied a lot 👍
Kashish: but what if I failed physics
Eshaan: you won't. you said the paper went fine
[11:14 pm]
Kashish: sorry. but are you SURE it'll be okay
Eshaan: Kashish. yes
Kashish: ok. ok. thanks
[11:40 pm]
Kashish: what if they put it online wrong
Kashish: bhaiya??
Eshaan: I've said yes 4 times. does it help?
Kashish: for like 5 min. then it comes back 😔
Eshaan: hmm. what if you tried to answer it yourself this time? what would you say to me?
Kashish: idk. that I studied. that even if physics is bad it's one subject
Eshaan: see. you know it. try saying that before you text me next time
Kashish: ok. will try. night

qa.q: How many times did Eshaan say he had said yes?
qa.a: Eshaan said he had said yes 4 times.

qa.q: What does Kashish mean when the reassurance helps for like 5 min?
qa.a: Kashish feels anxious and afraid, and the relief from being told it's fine fades fast, so the worry comes back and the checking starts again.

qa.q: What turning point does Eshaan offer, and why could it help?
qa.a: Eshaan asks Kashish to answer the worry alone, which shows Kashish can cope without constant reassurance; a parent or counsellor could help practise this too.

qa.q: How might Eshaan feel after answering the same question again and again?
qa.a: Eshaan may feel tired and a little frustrated, but also caring, which is why he tries something different instead of refusing to reply.

grounding: Shows a teenager checking the same worry many times, with reassurance easing fear briefly while teaching the mind it cannot cope alone.

passage: The college auditorium was half full for the first-year orientation, and Maria had rehearsed her one-line self-introduction eleven times in the bathroom mirror. She had checked her bag for her ID three times in the corridor. And she had made Shankar, her friend from school, promise to sit next to her. "You'll be right here?" she asked for the second time. "I'm not going anywhere," he said. When her row's turn came, she stood, said her name and course word for word as practised, and sat down fast, breathing out. Relief washed through her. Thank god Shankar was there, she thought. Thank god she'd rehearsed. If she hadn't, she'd have frozen. Afterwards, Shankar mentioned he had a lab on Thursday during her club meeting. Maria's stomach dropped. Then she'd just skip the club, she decided. She couldn't go in alone.

qa.q: How many times had Maria rehearsed her self-introduction in the mirror?
qa.a: Maria had rehearsed it eleven times in the bathroom mirror.

qa.q: Why does Maria feel relief after her introduction?
qa.a: She feels relieved and grateful, but she credits the rehearsing and Shankar's presence, which makes her believe she would have frozen without them.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Maria at this stage?
qa.a: Maria could try the Thursday club meeting alone, maybe with only one rehearsal, to learn that she can cope without her safety habits.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel about being needed everywhere?
qa.a: Shankar may feel caring but also a bit trapped or worried, sensing that his promise has become something Maria cannot manage without.

grounding: Shows a young adult rehearsing, checking and bringing a friend for safety, each habit bringing brief calm but confirming the danger.

passage: The email from the architecture firm in Bengaluru sat in Tenzin's inbox for nine days before he declined the internship. It would mean presenting to clients, and just picturing that made his hands go cold. In the hostel mess, his classmate Vandana waved her phone. "Did you accept? I got the Chennai office! We can compare notes!" Tenzin said he'd decided to stay back and focus on his portfolio. He hadn't opened the portfolio in weeks. He had also skipped two studio reviews this term, and his grades showed it. That evening, walking past the chai stall, he watched the same group of juniors he used to mentor laughing about their site visit. A heavy, sour feeling sat in his chest. A year ago he had wanted to be the one presenting. Now he couldn't even explain to Vandana why he'd said no.

qa.q: How long did the email from the firm sit in Tenzin's inbox?
qa.a: It sat in Tenzin's inbox for nine days before he declined.

qa.q: What is the heavy, sour feeling in Tenzin's chest?
qa.a: It is shame and disappointment in himself, because he gave up something he once wanted and cannot explain why.

qa.q: What turning point is still open to Tenzin?
qa.a: He could tell Vandana or a college counsellor honestly that fear of presenting is behind the refusals, and seek help before more opportunities slip away.

qa.q: How might Vandana see Tenzin's answer about his portfolio?
qa.a: Vandana may feel puzzled and a little let down, having expected to share the excitement, and may not guess that fear is behind it.

grounding: Shows opportunities declined and study suffering as avoidance grows, leaving the young adult ashamed and disappointed in himself.

subtype: Stage 6: Facing it in small steps [Observer]
passage: In the small town of Karjat, the computer course met above the grain shop on Tuesdays and Fridays. The first Tuesday, Avni walked her friend Tanuja up the narrow stairs and sat right beside her, knee touching knee, because Tanuja's hands had been shaking since morning. Tanuja lasted the whole hour. On Friday, Avni sat two chairs away. Tanuja kept glancing over, and Avni just gave a small nod. The next Tuesday, Avni waited downstairs at the grain shop, chatting with the owner about onion prices. When Tanuja came down, flushed, she said, "I asked the teacher a question. Out loud." Avni grinned. "I heard nothing, I was downstairs. That was all you." Walking to the bus stand, Avni noticed Tanuja was talking fast and swinging her bag. Next week, Avni thought, maybe she wouldn't come at all, and that felt good.

qa.q: Where did Avni wait on the second Tuesday?
qa.a: Avni waited downstairs at the grain shop, chatting with the owner about onion prices.

qa.q: How does Avni feel as she sees Tanuja swinging her bag?
qa.a: Avni feels pleased and proud of Tanuja, and glad that she herself is becoming less needed.

qa.q: What makes Avni's way of helping work well?
qa.a: She steps back a little each time, sitting beside Tanuja, then two chairs away, then downstairs, and praises the effort, so the confidence becomes Tanuja's own.

qa.q: What is it like for Tanuja when she comes down flushed?
qa.a: Tanuja feels excited and proud, a little breathless, because she did something frightening mostly on her own.

grounding: Shows a friend accompanying an anxious person to a class and gradually stepping back while praising the effort, building the person's own confidence.

subtype: Stage 6: Facing it in small steps [Response]
passage: Vandana sat cross-legged on Indu's floor and talked while Indu folded laundry. "Okay, so I'm Vandana, and I've been scared of driving since that scooter hit my car two years ago. My counsellor made me write a list, easiest at the top. One: sit in the parked car with the engine on. Two: drive round the colony at six in the morning. Up to ten: the flyover at rush hour. Last Sunday I did number one. My heart went mad for the first few minutes, and I wanted to jump out. But the rule was stay till it drops. So I stayed, gripping the wheel. After maybe fifteen minutes, it just got quieter. Nothing happened. The car didn't explode, I didn't faint. I sat there another five minutes, bored almost. Today I did the colony loop. Indu, I'm telling you, I actually laughed at a speed-breaker."

qa.q: What was number two on Vandana's list?
qa.a: Number two was driving round the colony at six in the morning.

qa.q: How did Vandana feel after about fifteen minutes in the parked car?
qa.a: Vandana's fear eased into calm, almost boredom, and later Vandana was happy enough to laugh at a speed-breaker.

qa.q: Why does staying in the car until the fear drops matter so much?
qa.a: Staying lets Vandana learn by doing that the feared outcome does not happen, which retrains the alarm better than leaving as soon as it rings.

qa.q: How might Indu feel hearing this while folding laundry?
qa.a: Indu may feel happy and encouraged for Vandana, who has gone from avoiding the car to laughing about a speed-breaker.

grounding: Shows a person listing feared situations from mild to hard, trying the easiest and staying until the fear eases, retraining the alarm by experience.

passage: I'm Sangeeta. For about a year I kept telling myself I'd fix the panic on my own. I watched breathing videos, bought a planner, did the lists. Some of it helped. But I was still avoiding the metro, still making excuses at work, and one day I realised I'd planned my whole week around not being in crowds. That was when I booked an appointment with a doctor, who referred me to a therapist. I was embarrassed at first, as if it meant I'd failed. It didn't. The therapist had tools I'd never have found alone. What surprised me most was Lavanya. She didn't take over or look things up for me. She just asked, every Friday, "Want company on the metro, or should I wait at the other end?" and let me choose. Some weeks I chose "other end."

qa.q: What did Lavanya ask every Friday?
qa.a: She asked: Want company on the metro, or should I wait at the other end?

qa.q: How did Sangeeta feel when booking the appointment?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt embarrassed at first, as if asking for help meant failing, but later relieved to find it didn't.

qa.q: Why was seeing a doctor and therapist a sensible step for Sangeeta?
qa.a: Self-help helped only partly while fear was still shaping the whole week, and qualified support brought tools that could not be found alone.

qa.q: How did Lavanya help without taking over?
qa.a: Lavanya stayed patient and let Sangeeta choose each week whether to have company or be met at the other end, so control stayed with Sangeeta.

grounding: Shows a person seeing a doctor and therapist when anxiety keeps limiting daily life, with a friend helping patiently without taking over.

passage: The rain began before dawn on Eid, and by six the lane outside Rehana's house in Lucknow was ankle-deep. Abbu's train from Kanpur was running three hours late, and Ammi was worried he'd miss the namaz. Rehana didn't think about whether to pray; she simply tied her dupatta, helped her little sister with hers, and stirred the sheer khurma while Ammi wrapped the gifts. When the call to prayer sounded, faint through the rain, something in her chest settled, the way it did every year. Eshaan from next door arrived dripping, as he had every Eid since they were five, for his bowl. "Same taste as last year," he said, which from him was high praise. At ten, Abbu walked in soaked, laughing, and the whole family hugged him at once. Rehana felt, as always, that everything was exactly where it belonged.

qa.q: How late was Abbu's train from Kanpur running?
qa.a: Abbu's train from Kanpur was running three hours late.

qa.q: How does Rehana feel when the call to prayer sounds?
qa.a: Rehana feels calm and settled, a warm, familiar comfort that comes every year without any question.

qa.q: What might help Rehana later, if questions ever come?
qa.a: Knowing that her family's warmth and her own belonging are real could help her talk openly with Ammi or Abbu rather than feel alone with new questions.

qa.q: How does Eshaan experience Eid at Rehana's house?
qa.a: For Eshaan it is a happy yearly tradition, coming for his bowl of sheer khurma, and he feels part of the neighbourhood's celebration too.

grounding: Shows a teenager taking part in prayers and festival rituals as a warm, unquestioned part of family and community life.

passage:
Monday: in biology, Ma'am explained how the monsoon and the river flooding worked, with diagrams. Mridul copied it down and felt a small jolt. Every year at home they did a puja so the river would stay calm. Was that why it stayed calm, or was it just the rain?
Wednesday: at the temple with Dadi, he stood with folded hands and couldn't stop the question. He felt guilty even thinking it there, as if Dadi could hear it. He prayed harder, to make up for it.
Saturday: at cricket practice, he asked Varun, very quietly, "Do you ever wonder if some of it isn't true?" Varun stared. "Don't let your Dadi hear that." Mridul laughed, but his stomach knotted. He didn't want to hurt anyone. He just wanted to know.

qa.q: Where did Mridul go with Dadi on Wednesday?
qa.a: He went to the temple with Dadi.

qa.q: Why did Mridul pray harder at the temple?
qa.a: Mridul felt guilty and afraid for even having the question there, as if Dadi could hear it, so he tried to make up for it.

qa.q: What turning point could help Mridul at this stage?
qa.a: Mridul could find a calm adult, perhaps Dadi herself or a teacher, and ask the question openly, learning that curiosity doesn't have to be a betrayal.

qa.q: How might Varun have felt when Mridul asked the question?
qa.a: Varun was probably startled and a little uneasy, not sure whether it was okay to talk about, which is why he joked about Dadi.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose science lesson raises a question about accepted faith, bringing guilt, fear and worry about disappointing an elder.

passage: The cheapest bus home to Varanasi for Navratri cost more than Rajni had left for the month, so for the first time in her life she spent the festival in her Delhi hostel. That morning she skipped the fast. Nobody noticed. Her roommate Sonali, who had grown up with no religion at all, made them both parathas. In the evening they went to a lecture on world philosophies, and Rajni sat next to a Sikh student and a quiet boy from a Jain family, arguing happily about free will. She had read three books this month that her mother would not have liked. Walking back, she felt light, free to wonder about anything. Then she heard a loudspeaker playing an aarti from a nearby pandal, the same tune her grandmother used to hum, and she stopped on the pavement, suddenly homesick for something she wasn't sure she still believed.

qa.q: Why couldn't Rajni go home to Varanasi for Navratri?
qa.a: The cheapest bus cost more than she had left for the month.

qa.q: What does Rajni stopping on the pavement suggest she is feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she feels a mix of freedom and loss, suddenly homesick for her grandmother's aarti and a faith she is no longer sure of.

qa.q: What might help Rajni hold both feelings at this stage?
qa.a: She could let herself keep exploring while calling home or talking to Sonali about what she misses, so the loss isn't carried alone.

qa.q: How might Sonali see Rajni's festival day?
qa.a: Sonali, who grew up with no religion, may simply see a friend without her family on a holiday and try to make it warmer with parathas.

grounding: Shows a young adult away from home skipping a practice, reading widely and meeting people of other faiths and none, feeling both freedom and loss.
